children.value: Moku is an auto-layout planner: drop a widget on a screen and the layout re-solves right there, the same way a scroll view actually expands to fill whatever space is left. It is not a freehand drawing tool — every frame you see is the real layout.

The Boards screen opens on "Your boards" — a home view with a recent-boards list and a row of start buttons. Alongside a plain New board, one New from template button per shipped applet mints a ready-made board copied from that app's real screens, so you can study or remix a working design instead of starting blank. The first eight (Taskly, Dispatch, Korea travel access, Wikipick, Car-free access ranking, Notes, bublie, Chronos) stay pinned first; the rest are ordered by the applet's own catalog category (Productivity, Planning & lists, Life, Finance, Security, Maps & cities, Analytics, Creative, Media, Games, Developer) so applets in the same family sit next to each other in the button row. Once you have opened a board, the same New/template choices are always one tap away from the ▾ New menu above the board list.
Tap + Screen on the board to add a new device frame. Drag a frame by its header chip to move it around the board; pinch or use two fingers to pan and zoom the whole board.

Tap + Component to add a frameless piece instead — a fixed-width block that sizes itself to whatever you drop on it, with no device frame around it. Useful for a reusable header, card, or nav strip you are mocking up on its own rather than inside a full screen.

The widget strip along the top of the board holds all 13 kinds. Drag a chip onto a screen to insert it into the region under your drop point (top/body/bottom/overlay); tap a chip instead to add it to the end of the selected screen's default region.

Each kind has a default size behaviour: fixed widgets (titlebar, searchbar, tabs, bottomnav, fab) keep a set height; wrap widgets (text, card, image, buttonrow) size to their content; fill widgets (scrollview, list, settings) stretch to share whatever vertical space is left in the body, splitting it evenly with any other fill widgets on the same screen. Tap a widget to select it and use the quick actions bar to rename, delete, reorder, cycle its region, or override its size intent.

Drop the Columns chip to add a two-column container — the block a sidebar-and-main layout, a header with a logo on one side and a nav on the other, or a row of cards needs. Drag any other chip into one of its columns to fill that cell; drag a block back out to return it to the screen's normal top-level flow. A column cannot hold another Columns block — nest one level only.

Use “Make variant” on a screen to project it to another device frame (phone/tablet/web). The variant starts as a copy of the widgets, laid out fresh at the new frame size, then lives independently — edits on one side do not sync to the other.

Select a widget and choose “link to screen…”, then tap a target screen to create a flow — shown as a light curved arrow on the board. Toggle Play to try it: tapping a linked widget animates the board over to its target screen and briefly highlights the frame.

The review icon (top right) switches a board between Edit and design review. In review, every frame shows a status dot — approved, proposed, or changes — and a legend at the bottom counts them live. Tap a frame to open it full-screen: swipe between frames, tap a numbered pin to read its note, Approve with one tap, or Request changes (which asks for a note first, so a change request always says what needs to change). Tap the + note button, then tap a spot on the frame, to drop a new pin there. A design project can hold either kind of frame side by side — a captured image (for a mockup made elsewhere) or a live native Moku screen — and a live frame gets its own Edit button in the review screen that opens it straight in the ordinary editor: any edit you make there is a normal board change, so your edits are the design, not a separate copy of it. Sticky notes float on the board itself for anything that is not tied to one frame.
